migrationNotes: Spine: a bookshop sign is a test each book passes or fails, and we write that test for the shop's orders, then meet its awkward cases in turn (a missing amount, two tests at once, a value on the line, a list of values).
Left out of the lesson (still in the course): sql-filter-the-rows-8 (WHERE amount > 50 over 30, 60, NULL and 90). The first teaching screens and sql-filter-the-rows-1 cover the same idea.

lesson.title: Write the condition you mean

steps.headline: A test that each row passes or fails

lead.text: Take a shop sign that says 'Under £10'. It is a test you can apply to any book, and every book either passes or fails it. A book priced at exactly 10 pounds fails, because 10 is not under 10. A test like that is called a condition.

In a query the condition goes after WHERE, and the database keeps the rows that pass it and drops the rest. WHERE amount > 50 keeps the orders worth more than 50. The comparison signs are = for equal, <> for not equal, > and < for greater and less, and >= and <= for greater or equal and less or equal. The two signs with an equals sign include the line itself. The picture sets two of them side by side.

afterFigure.text: Both queries read the same orders. The first keeps the two orders worth exactly 20, and the second drops them because 20 is not more than 20. Which sign you want depends on the sentence in your head. 'At least' and 'at most' include the line, while 'more than' and 'less than' leave it out.

queries.label: At least 20
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE amount >= 20 ORDER BY id;

queries.label: More than 20
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE amount > 20 ORDER BY id;

lead.text: Each book on the shelf either passes the sign's test or fails it.

One order in the shop has no amount at all. Order 106 holds NULL, and a test on an unknown value can't come out true, because the database has no way to show that an unknown number is above or below anything. WHERE keeps only the rows whose condition is true, so a row with a missing amount is dropped by every test on that amount, including tests such as amount <= 40 that look as if it might survive.

To find the missing amounts themselves you need a different test. amount = NULL doesn't work, because nothing is ever equal to an unknown value, not even another unknown one. SQL has its own wording for this: amount IS NULL keeps the rows whose amount is missing, and amount IS NOT NULL keeps the rest.

afterFigure.text: Look for order 106 in the picture. It is missing from the first result, and it appears only when the condition asks for a missing amount directly.

queries.label: Amount at most 40
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE amount <= 40 ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Missing amount
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE amount IS NULL ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Amount known
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE amount IS NOT NULL ORDER BY id;

lead.text: Of the six orders, one has no known amount.

queries.label: At least 40
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE amount >= 40 ORDER BY id;

queries.label: At least 80
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE amount >= 80 ORDER BY id;

lead.text: A shop owner rarely wants a single test. She might want the orders that are paid and also worth at least 40, or the orders that are paid or worth at least 40. Two conditions can be joined into one rule with AND and OR. With AND a row has to pass both tests, and with OR a row has to pass at least one of them.

That makes AND the stricter word. Adding a test with AND can only remove rows, because each row has more to satisfy, while adding a test with OR can only let more rows in. A missing amount still can't pass the amount test, so a row with one survives an OR only by passing the other test.

afterFigure.text: Order 106 shows the difference in the picture. It is a Lamp with no known amount, so it fails the AND query. It appears in the OR query, because it passes the item test.

queries.label: Lamp AND at least 40
queries.sql: SELECT id, item, amount FROM orders WHERE item = 'Lamp' AND amount >= 40 ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Lamp OR at least 40
queries.sql: SELECT id, item, amount FROM orders WHERE item = 'Lamp' OR amount >= 40 ORDER BY id;

lead.text: A row must pass every test that AND joins.

queries.label: Both conditions
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount, status FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid' AND amount >= 40 ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Either condition
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount, status FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid' OR amount >= 40 ORDER BY id;

lead.text: With OR, a row stays when either test is true.

steps.headline: On the line and between lines

lead.text: Back to the line itself. A range such as 'from 20 to 40' has two ends, and the question is whether the ends count. BETWEEN 20 AND 40 includes both of them, so it means the same as amount >= 20 AND amount <= 40. Writing amount > 20 AND amount < 40 leaves both ends out.

Say the rule aloud before you write it. 'From 20 to 40' and 'between 20 and 40' usually mean that the ends count, while 'over 20 and under 40' means they don't. The comparison signs are the exact version of that wording. The picture runs both versions over the shop's orders.

afterFigure.text: As before, an order with a missing amount passes neither query. The ends matter whenever a value can land exactly on one, and in the shop several amounts do.

queries.label: Ends counted
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE amount BETWEEN 20 AND 40 ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Ends left out
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE amount > 20 AND amount < 40 ORDER BY id;

lead.text: Compare a range that counts its ends with one that leaves them out.

Sometimes the condition isn't a range. The shop might want the orders for Books or Lamps. One way is item = 'Book' OR item = 'Lamp'. A shorter way is IN, which keeps a row whose value matches anything in a list, as in item IN ('Book', 'Lamp'). Text goes inside single quotes.
The picture shows two lists run over the same orders.

afterFigure.text: This condition looks at the item, so the unknown amount on order 106 makes no difference to it. The order is a Lamp, and it passes. Conditions on different columns don't affect each other, which is why a missing amount matters only to tests that read the amount.

queries.label: Book or Lamp
queries.sql: SELECT id, item FROM orders WHERE item IN ('Book', 'Lamp') ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Desk or Lamp
queries.sql: SELECT id, item FROM orders WHERE item IN ('Desk', 'Lamp') ORDER BY id;

lead.text: A list of accepted values is another kind of condition.

queries.label: Book or Lamp
queries.sql: SELECT id, item FROM orders WHERE item IN ('Book', 'Lamp') ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Missing amount
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE amount IS NULL ORDER BY id;

lesson.orientation: Use SQL conditions to select exactly the rows your question requires.
lesson.nextAction: Apply the idea to the next query.

blocks.text: A bookshop puts a sign on one shelf. It says 'Books at least £20', and the shelf holds books priced at 5, 12, 20, 25 and 30 pounds. A customer reads the sign and works out which of the books it covers.

The sign is a test, and each book either passes it or doesn't. Most books are clear. The book at exactly 20 pounds is the one that needs a moment's thought, because it sits on the line that the test draws.

A query carries tests like this, and it can apply one to a table of many thousands of orders as easily as to a shelf of five books. This lesson shows how to write the test you mean. The hard cases are the value that sits exactly on the line and the order whose price nobody knows. It also shows how to join two tests into one rule.

intro.promise: By the end you'll write conditions that keep exactly the rows you mean, including at the boundary and for unknown values.

recap.keyIdea: WHERE keeps the rows whose condition is true. Choose the comparison, the boundary and AND or OR for exactly the rows you mean.

blocks.text: Back at the shelf, the sign's test became a condition you could write. You counted 3 orders of at least 40 and 2 that were paid and large, and you saw that an order with an unknown amount passed no comparison.

recap.nextHook: A condition decides which rows stay, and it says nothing about their order. Five runners and a stopwatch begin the next lesson, because a medal depends on who finished first.

hints: Which amounts are 40 or more?
A comparison with an unknown amount is never true.
Go down the amount column and count each known amount that is 40 or higher. An amount of exactly 40 counts.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Orders 101, 103 and 104 satisfy the comparison; 106 has a missing amount.

questions.onCorrect: 3. The comparison keeps amounts of 40 and above, boundary included. The unknown amount never passes.

misconceptions.feedback: Check the boundary. At least 40 includes an amount of exactly 40.
One amount is unknown. A comparison with an unknown amount is never true.

questions.prompt: How many orders satisfy status = 'paid' AND amount >= 40?
hints: A row has to pass both tests, the one on status and the one on amount.
List the paid orders first, then check each of them against the amount test.
Cross out any paid order with an amount below 40.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Only paid orders 101 and 103 also have amount at least 40.

questions.onCorrect: 2. AND needs both tests to pass, so only paid orders of at least 40 remain.

misconceptions.feedback: That ignores the status test. Every row must also be paid.
That is what OR would give. Here a row has to pass both tests.

questions.prompt: Which values can pass amount BETWEEN 20 AND 40?
hints: BETWEEN includes its two boundaries.

acceptedIdeas: Values from 20 through 40, including both ends
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: BETWEEN includes both endpoints, so 20 and 40 pass as well as values between them. An unknown amount does not pass this comparison.

choices.label: Values from 20 through 40, including both ends

questions.onCorrect: The range includes both ends. BETWEEN 20 AND 40 keeps 20, 40 and everything between.

misconceptions.feedback: Look at the two end values. Does BETWEEN keep a row at exactly 20?
There is also an upper end. Values above it fail.

questions.prompt: How many orders have item IN ('Book', 'Lamp')?
hints: An item can match either value in the list.
An unknown amount doesn't stop an item from matching.
Count the Book orders and the Lamp orders separately, then add the two counts.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two Book orders and two Lamp orders make four.

questions.onCorrect: 4. IN accepts any value in its list, so two Book rows and two Lamp rows pass.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts one of the two names only. A row passes if its item is either one.
That is every order. Only rows whose item is in the list pass.

questions.prompt: How many orders satisfy amount > 20 AND amount < 80?
hints: Both inequalities are strict.
Count known amounts strictly between the boundaries.
The known amounts are 80, 20, 80, 40 and 20. Keep only strict interior values.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Only order 104 has amount 40; the 20 and 80 boundaries are excluded.

questions.onCorrect: 1. Both comparisons are strict, so the amounts 20 and 80 are out and only 40 stays.

misconceptions.feedback: Strict comparisons drop the amounts exactly on the lines.
Check the amounts again. Which known ones sit strictly between the lines?

questions.prompt: Which condition finds an unknown amount?
hints: SQL provides a missing-value predicate.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Use amount IS NULL to test for a missing value. Equality to NULL does not evaluate to true in SQL.

questions.onCorrect: amount IS NULL. Nothing equals NULL, so an unknown amount needs its own test.

misconceptions.feedback: Nothing equals NULL, not even NULL. That test is never true.
Zero is a known amount. An unknown amount is a different state.

questions.prompt: A bookshop sign says 'Books at least £20'. The shelf holds books priced 5, 12, 20, 25 and 30 pounds. How many books does the sign cover?
hints: Which prices are at or above the line?
'At least' counts a price sitting exactly on the line.
Count the book on the line as well as the dearer ones.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: At least £20 covers the books at 20, 25 and 30 pounds: three books.

questions.onCorrect: 3. A condition has a boundary, and 'at least' keeps the books exactly on it. A query condition works the same way.

misconceptions.feedback: The sign says at least. A book priced exactly at the line is covered too.

questions.prompt: WHERE amount > 50 is applied to the amounts 30, 60, NULL and 90. Which rows stay?
hints: Which of these amounts are above the line, and what happens to the unknown one?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 60 and 90 are greater than 50. 30 is not, and a comparison with NULL is never true.

questions.onCorrect: 60 and 90. A row stays only when its condition is true, and a comparison with an unknown amount never is.

misconceptions.feedback: An unknown amount cannot be shown to be above 50, so its row is dropped.
60 is above 50 too. Check each amount against the condition.

questions.prompt: A query keeps the orders where status = 'paid' OR amount >= 40. Order 102 is paid and its amount is only 20. Why is it kept?
hints: Does a row have to pass both tests, or only one?

acceptedIdeas: OR keeps a row when either condition is true, and it is paid.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Order 102 is paid. With OR, passing one test is enough.

questions.onCorrect: OR keeps a row when either test is true. Order 102 passes the status test, so its amount does not matter.

choices.label: OR keeps a row when either condition is true, and it is paid.

misconceptions.feedback: Conditions are exact. A row passes or fails; nearly does not count.
The query says OR. AND would need both tests to pass.

questions.prompt: The amounts are 10, 20, 30, NULL and 40. How many pass amount BETWEEN 20 AND 40?
hints: Does BETWEEN count the two end values?
An unknown amount passes no comparison.
List the amounts from 20 up to 40 that are known.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 20, 30 and 40 pass. 10 is below the range and NULL passes nothing.

questions.onCorrect: 3. BETWEEN includes both ends, and the unknown amount never passes.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts only the amount strictly inside the range. BETWEEN also keeps the two end values.
One of those five is unknown, and an unknown amount never passes a comparison.
